content: A breast abscess is an uncommon infectious condition characterized by a localized collection of pus beneath the skin of the breast. It is often considered a complicated form of breast inflammation, also known as mastitis. In 1841, Dr. Jonathan Toogood documented a case of breast abscess, marking an early historical reference to this condition. Breast abscesses are classified based on their anatomical location, including subcutaneous, subareolar, interlobular, central, and retromammary types. They are also categorized by the lactation status of the patient, either lactational or non-lactational. The pathophysiology of a breast abscess typically involves progression from untreated mastitis. The condition is most commonly caused by a bacterial infection, particularly Staphylococcus aureus, which enters through injured breast skin. This bacterium produces enzymes and toxins that lead to necrosis of breast tissue. In response, white blood cells gather in the affected area and produce antibodies to combat the bacteria. However, this immune response can also damage the surrounding soft tissue, contributing to abscess formation. The underlying mechanisms of breast abscess formation are closely related to those of mastitis. Breast abscesses are primarily caused by bacterial pathogens, with Staphylococcus aureus being the most common. In some cases, fungal infections, such as Candida species transmitted through an infant's mouth, may also be responsible. The pathogens involved are often the same as those causing mastitis. These organisms can be classified into gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria. It is essential to differentiate breast abscesses from other conditions that cause breast swelling, such as mastitis, inflammatory breast cancer, galactocele, plugged ducts, Mondor's syndrome, and fibroadenoma. Breast abscesses are rare, with an incidence of 3,000 to 11,000 cases per 100,000 patients with mastitis. There is no significant data on the overall prevalence of this condition. The most critical risk factor for developing a breast abscess is trauma to the breast. Other contributing factors include duct ectasia, obesity, diabetes mellitus, and insect bites. If left untreated, a breast abscess may rupture through the skin. Complications can include milk fistula formation and antibioma. With appropriate treatment, the prognosis is generally favorable, although recurrence is possible. Patients with a breast abscess often notice a breast mass or lump. They may have a current or past history of breast infection (mastitis). Symptoms include fever, fatigue, skin induration, and nipple discharge. On physical examination, patients typically present with breast tenderness, swelling, redness, and warmth of the overlying skin. The diagnosis of a breast abscess is primarily clinical and does not rely on laboratory findings. However, cultures of milk or pus may be obtained to guide antibiotic therapy. Electrocardiograms (EKG) and chest X-rays do not show significant changes in patients with breast abscesses. Similarly, CT scans are not routinely used for diagnosis but may be performed to rule out other conditions, such as breast cancer. Ultrasound is a critical imaging modality for diagnosing and guiding the surgical management of breast abscesses. Mammography may also be used to differentiate between a breast abscess and breast cancer. Treatment of a breast abscess involves antibiotics, such as flucloxacillin, dicloxacillin, or erythromycin, as a supportive measure alongside surgical interventions. These antibiotics also help prevent recurrence. The first-line surgical treatment for a breast abscess is ultrasound-guided needle aspiration or surgical drainage. Prevention of breast abscesses focuses on reducing risk factors and improving hygiene, particularly in lactating patients. Emphasis is placed on maintaining proper hygiene for both the mother and infant. Breastfeeding is encouraged to continue after abscess drainage to prevent recurrence.
